arc-a.verdict: A great two-second toy on the current brand, but the sticker idea is only in the hero and the closing panel. The page between them is stock dark SaaS.
arc-a.loved: Amber stickers of soft words ('so i think', 'honestly just', 'lol') peeling off an ultramarine stage. Blue against amber is the brand's two existing colours at full contrast, and the stickers work as real merch: a sticker sheet of soft words, or a peel GIF for social.
problems: Two metaphors for one thing. The headline uses the amber squiggle (the mark the app really draws), but the demo turns soft words into stickers. Nobody sees stickers after signing up, so the hero teaches a UI that doesn't exist.
Below the hero the stickers vanish into generic dark SaaS: bento cards and a checklist pricing table. About 70% of the page could belong to any dark tool.
A white 'H' in a rounded blue tile is the most generic app mark there is. Nothing in the logo carries the peel or the sharp-line idea.
The layout is a template: a full blue stage, a centred white serif headline, two pills and a product card below. Without the peel animation it has almost nothing distinctive.
arc-a.fix: Pick one metaphor. Either make the sticker the soft-word token everywhere (in the app, squiggled words lift as stickers when you tap Sharpen, and the same stickers carry section breaks and tags), or drop the stickers and peel the squiggle itself.

arc-b.verdict: The tightest type grammar in the round (heavy grotesk for sharp, italic serif for soft), built from a 2025 template kit, and it would cost a full rebrand.
arc-b.loved: Every heading acts out the product: 'Every rewrite / comes with a receipt.', 'It drafts. / You press send.' The till receipt (move, why, kept, cut, words) is a product-true artefact people could share.
problems: A total rebrand. It drops ultramarine, Newsreader, dark-first and the logo, so a new user lands in an app that shares nothing with this page except amber.

Bricolage Grotesque, Instrument Serif italic, cream paper, acid lime and pastel bento tiles are the default Framer kit of 2025. Any competitor can buy this look as a template, so only the grammar is ownable.
The lime fishhook 'J' tile reads as the letter J and leans on hook-and-bait, i.e. clickbait. That is exactly the wrong signal for a product whose promise is 'your facts stay'.
Lime only works behind ink, so the hero colour can't carry an ad on its own. The pastel tiles dilute it further.
arc-b.fix: Keep the soft-italic vs sharp-heavy grammar and the receipt, but rebuild them on the current ultramarine and amber, with Newsreader italic as the soft voice and a heavy Inter as the sharp one. The idea survives without the rebrand bill.

awwwards-b.verdict: The richest brand world in the round: the blue pencil finally gives the arbitrary SaaS blue a meaning. But it drops the squiggle and needs a second, light-first brand.
awwwards-b.loved: The ultramarine becomes the editor's blue pencil ('to blue-pencil' means to edit). The pencil is a physical object ('Hookworthy Blue Pencil No. 28') that can be swag, outdoor ads, a social format (proof marks drawn over real posts) and even a pricing gesture ($12 circled in pencil).
problems: It swaps the amber wavy underline, the one mark the app actually draws, for a flat highlighter plus proofreader's marks. The site's signature never appears in the product.
'Write it rough. Post it sharp.' is about writing in general, and Grammarly, Hemingway or Typefully could run it too. The first line, the brand's whole unit, gets pushed to the footer.

There are four faces, including Caveat handwriting on every annotation. Fake handwriting will look like clip-art in ads, in other languages and in the UI, and it will date first. The proof cards also sit half-empty at rest because the set line hasn't animated in.
Newsprint and Garamond speak to newsletter writers, but crypto and trading writers, the first audience, live in dark mode. A light-first site next to a dark-first app is a second brand to maintain.
awwwards-b.fix: Keep the pencil and the galley proof, but set them in Newsreader and have the pencil draw the marks the app really uses: the amber squiggle and a blue strike. Replace the headline with one that names the first line.

apple-b.verdict: Clean and confident, and almost nothing in it is ownable. Inter on a blue field with white post cards is how the networks themselves look.
apple-b.loved: 'Write the line they stop for.' with one crisp post standing still in a drifting, blurred feed, its old line struck through above the sharp one. It is the clearest single picture of the outcome.
problems: A blue field with white post cards and an Inter headline is the visual language of Bluesky, LinkedIn and old Twitter. In a feed this ad blends into the platform's own UI instead of stopping the thumb.
It drops Newsreader, the only thing that set the current brand apart from sans-serif SaaS. What's left (an 'h' tile, Inter, white cards) is unownable.
The drifting feed is a low-contrast metaphor. In the first half-second it's blurred blue noise, and the idea only lands once you read the post.
There is no brand device that repeats down the page besides the blue, so the sections could be shuffled into any startup's site.
apple-b.fix: Keep 'one still post in a moving feed' as a motion-ad format, but move it into the current brand: a dark feed, the post set in Newsreader, and amber squiggles on the soft ghost posts so the sharp one is the only clean line.

typefully-a.verdict: The visuals are dark-SaaS house style, but the brand idea is the most ownable in the round, and it is built from marks the app already draws.
typefully-a.loved: 'Make it hookworthy.' turns the product name into the adjective, a line no competitor can ever say. The split wordmark (bold 'hook' with a blue rule, italic 'worthy') acts it out. Together with 'See the squiggle?' it sets up a two-mark system taken straight from the product: an amber wavy line for soft, a blue straight rule for sharp.
problems: Remove the wordmark and Typefully, Linear or Raycast could wear this page: near-black, serif headings with a grey second line, a sticky feature index.
Every section uses the same white/grey two-line heading. It's coherent but monotone, with no visual peak between the hero and the blue closing panel.
There's no iconic object for ads or swag. The receipt is the only shareable artefact, and its torn-edge card is cut off at the 900px fold.
Two taglines compete: 'They read one line. Make it hookworthy.' and the closing 'Good ideas die in bad first lines.' Pick which one is the brand line and which is the sign-off.
typefully-a.fix: Make the Sharpen receipt the brand's signature artefact: a share-ready card (torn edge, mono, the move named) that users can post from the app. Use it as the hero visual for ads and social, and pull it fully above the fold.

pickWhy: It's the only finalist where the brand name itself is the promise ('Make it hookworthy') and the identity is built from marks the app already draws (amber squiggle, blue rule, receipt), so it costs nothing to adopt and strengthens the product on every screen. Its weakness, generic dark-SaaS visuals, can be fixed with a campaign layer. The rebrands' weaknesses (cost, audience fit, the lost squiggle) are structural.
combo: Use typefully-a's line, split wordmark, squiggle/rule pair and receipt as the core. Add awwwards-b's blue pencil as the campaign and illustration language (ultramarine proof marks drawn over real posts, the pencil as swag) and arc-a's peel-off soft-word stickers as merch, both drawn in the app's own amber squiggle.
